The Weilüe, a Chinese text composed in the early third century CE, describes the Roman Empire (Da Qin) as a distant kingdom located west of Parthia and the Great Sea, accessible by sea voyage from Parthia in as little as two months with favorable winds, though the journey could take up to three years without wind. [S1] According to this source, the Roman Empire "has more than four hundred smaller cities and towns" and "extends several thousand li in all directions," with its capital located near a river and surrounded by stone walls. [S1] A later Chinese historical text records that in 166 CE, the king of Da Qin sent envoys bearing elephant tusks, rhinoceros horn, and turtle shell, marking what the Chinese source describes as "the very first time there was [direct] communication" between the two countries. [S3]

The Weilüe, a Chinese text composed in the early third century CE, describes the Roman Empire (Da Qin) as a distant kingdom located "west of Anxi (Parthia) and Tiaozhi (Characene and Susiana), and west of the Great Sea," accessible by sea from Parthian territory in a journey that could take anywhere from two months to three years depending on wind conditions. [S1] According to this source, the Roman Empire "has more than four hundred smaller cities and towns" and "extends several thousand li in all directions," with its capital located "close to the mouth of a river" and surrounded by "outer walls of the city" made of stone. [S1] A later Chinese historical record, the Hou Hanshu, documents that in 166 CE "the king of Da Qin (the Roman Empire), Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus), sent envoys" to the Chinese court bearing "elephant tusks, rhinoceros horn, and turtle shell," and notes that "this was the very first time there was [direct] communication [between the two countries]." [S3]
